content.thinking:
I need to plan out realistic proportions for this pixel-art monster truck model — roughly 1.7m diameter tires, a 3.5m wide and 5m long body, about 3.4m tall overall — then set up the chassis and wheel joints accordingly.

Wheel joints hinge on the truck's axis with dedicated steering joints for the front wheels, while the body panels get boxy geometry and painted colors for that chunky pixel-art look. For the tires, I'm using chunky cylinders with extra segments and figuring out how to fake tread detail with cell painting since tileBox won't work on curved surfaces.

Still building tread geometry...

I'm sizing the lugs so the tire's outer radius stays under 0.91 to keep ground sink minimal, then setting up a hub cylinder of radius 0.42.

For the rim, I'm planning a pixel-art circular texture applied to a disc on the wheel's outer face, with a dark outer ring, light rim, and bolt pattern, plus speckled dithering on the tire's dark core for texture.

Now I'm laying out axle positions and wheel track width — settling on a 3.6m track with wheels centered at x=±1.45 spanning 1.1 to 1.8, matching real monster truck proportions, then sketching the chassis rails and suspension setup with coilover shocks at each wheel corner.

Writing shock and spring geometry...

Now I'm planning the truck body sitting high atop the frame, pickup-style with distinct hood, cab, and bed sections — roughly 2.0 wide, with hood spanning z 0.7 to 2.3, cab from -0.7 to 0.7, and bed from -2.3 to -0.7.

I'm picking a vivid blue body color with orange flame decals and white stripes, planning to generate the flames as a pixel-art texture with a wavy height function and place them on side planes near x=±1.

I need to work out the orientation carefully: viewed from each side, "left" in the image maps to front or rear depending on which side you're facing, so I'm checking whether to mirror the texture on the opposite side plane so flames consistently point backward from the front wheel arch on both sides.

I'm now planning the body structure around a chassis root joint, with door hinge joints positioned at the front edges and a tailgate hinge at the rear, then thinking through how to build wheel arches and hood using simple box segments since true cutouts aren't possible with boxes.

I'm working out the fender flare geometry — thin plates arching over the wheels with lips at front and back, checking that the body width and tire positions don't clash, then starting to list out all the parts for the frame.

Now I'm defining the frame rails, crossmembers, and axle components — dark boxes for the rails, spaced crossmembers, and cylinders for the axle shafts with a pumpkin-shaped differential sphere at center, plus planning panhard bars.

Next I'm working out the suspension and body shell: four-link rod connections between axle and frame using thin cylindrical rods, shock placements, then shaping the body itself — rocker panels, hood, cab, and bed sections as stacked boxes positioned along the vehicle's length and height.

Now I'm detailing the bed and cab structure: hollow bed walls, floor, tailgate with a hinge, a roll bar with lights mounted behind the cab, and the cab's lower body box topped by a greenhouse made of angled window panes and a roof slab, positioning the windshield and rear window with appropriate tilts.

For the interior, I'm deciding to keep it minimal — opaque glass hides most details, so I'll just sketch basic seats, dash, and steering wheel, and open up the door windows slightly so a glimpse of a seat and a tiny driver silhouette peeks through.

Now I'm planning the code structure: small helper functions for creating boxes with consistent bone/joint defaults, a modest color palette (~25 flat colors), and a cell-based paint system for the body that darkens near the bottom, adds mud splatter near the wheels, and scatters light scratch speckles across panels for wear.

I'm sizing the paint texture atlas at 2048px to keep texel density reasonable for the body's painted surface area, applying similar dithered dark paint with mud bias to the tires and lugs, and sketching out pixel-art decals -- a numeral "7" for the door and a grille/headlight texture for the front fascia.

Now I'm adding more detail pieces: chrome exhaust stacks with glowing orange tips behind the cab, a roof light bar with glow boxes, rear red light clusters and a license plate texture, plus door mirrors. I'm also setting up the wheel steering joints, defining each wheel's position and parent relationships for the front steerable pairs.

Writing joint hierarchy code...

Still writing the pixel fill logic...

Adding axle cylinders at the wheel hubs, then working out fender flare plates that need to arch over each wheel's span along the z-axis.

Yes, the flare connects to the body. Now I'm positioning the wheels relative to the hood and chassis—front wheels sit outboard of the body at x1.1–1.8, with the rocker panel and hood boxes defining the body paint sections above the undercarriage, plus a hood scoop bulge for detail.

Adding chrome blower and injector stacks...

Working out the windshield's angled geometry...

Then I'll add a rear window glass box and a rear cab wall beneath it.

C-pillars become small boxes flanking the rear window, and I'm placing door hinge joints along the side with the door panel geometry spanning the window opening.

Still positioning door panels...

Still sizing the flame decal...

Tuning the flame tongue curve...

Now I'm working out the bed geometry, sizing the floor box and side walls so their heights line up properly with the cab's lower edge.

I'll texture the bed floor with a ridged tile pattern for corrugation, and add cargo items like a toolbox and cooler for detail. Now I'm thinking about the rear fender flares.

For the interior, I'm placing seat boxes with bases and backs, a dashboard, and a steering wheel torus, then positioning a driver figure on the left side with torso and head boxes built from simple geometric primitives.

The head is clipping the roof, so I'm raising the roof height and adjusting the greenhouse/pillar dimensions to give proper clearance, recalculating the windshield's angle and center point accordingly, and nudging the overall vehicle height up slightly to accommodate a light bar on top.

I'm designing the driver figure with a pixel-art face texture on a plane mounted in front of a skin-colored head box, adding a red helmet with a visor, positioning the driver on the left side near the door, and adding a tilted torus steering wheel in front of them.

Now I'm laying out the roof-mounted light bar with glowing light boxes, plus headlight glow elements and a front fascia/bumper assembly near the hood.

I'm positioning the front bumper and grille so they align with the tire and hood dimensions without clipping, then adding tail lights, a rear bumper, and a tow hitch at the back of the vehicle, and I'm about to work out the exhaust stack placement.

Now I'm modeling the exhaust stacks as vertical cylinders near the bed front with flared conical tops and small glowing orange discs inside, then adding suspension details like shock springs and a steering tie rod linking the front wheel pivots.

I'm also laying out drivetrain shafts connecting the front differential to the transfer case and rear axle, placing the transfer case as a hidden box near the engine, and hanging a silver fuel tank box beneath the frame rails behind the cab, adjusting its position and width so it fits between the rails without clipping.

Now I'm roughing out the suspension links—adding front and rear 4-link rods between the axles and frame—and positioning the rear differential as a slightly flattened sphere with axle tubes extending to each side, plus a cylindrical axle shaft and wheel hub geometry to cap off each end.

Working through part counts, I'm planning the tire assembly: a core cylinder, 14 alternating lug blocks spaced around the circumference with slight tangential offsets for a chevron tread pattern, a sidewall decal, and hub caps per wheel, keeping rotations simple by rotating lugs about the x-axis. I'm also thinking about adding mud splatter detailing near the bottom of each wheel for a worn, off-road look.

For the mud effect I'm blending darker tire paint colors with randomized mud patches concentrated near the lower portion of the tires and sprinkled onto the body, then adding simple mudguard flaps behind the rear wheels with a yellow stripe. I'm also double-checking floor clearance by computing the lowest point of a rotated lug at the bottom of the wheel to make sure it only sinks a tiny, acceptable fraction into the ground.

Now I'm setting up the joint skeleton: a root chassis joint, steering joints for the front wheels, wheel hinges, door and tailgate hinges, and a hinge joint for the steering wheel, each defined with parent, position, direction, and role. I'm also sketching overall vehicle dimensions and starting a helper function for creating sized, colored boxes.

Writing geometry helpers...

Settling the shock top near the body floor for a tilted spring-and-rod look, with a chrome shock body and thinner rod topped by spring coils. Now I'm moving on to textures -- flame decal (flipped), pixel-art number 7, grille, and keeping the glass flat-colored rather than adding a glint.

For the glass texture I'll use a pixel-diagonal pattern on a blue-ish base with a white streak, applied to the box geometry so the tint carries through. I'm skipping the plate lettering, but adding decals: white racing stripes on the hood (positioned to avoid the blower) and matching stripes on the roof, plus a number-7 roundel on the doors built from a pixel texture -- a white circle with a black "7" digit stamped in the center.

I'm working out placement details: the roundel orientation on the doors so the number reads correctly without mirroring, aligning the door decal plane just outside the door skin, and positioning flame decals on the rocker panels to coincide with the bed side wall, centering them around mid-body height.

For the fender flares, I'm checking that the flare box intersects the rocker only at its inner edge so the flare looks like it's emerging from the rocker rather than overlapping it, and adjusting the flare height upward slightly to keep clearance above the tire while still touching the rocker edge.

Now I'm defining the grille texture as a bordered chrome frame with alternating vertical bars and a central emblem stripe, then moving on to setting the tire sidewall decals and final chrome color values.

Writing wheel hub texture...

Still refining tire texture...

Thinking through added details: a gold hub protrusion at the wheel center, plus a front winch assembly with bumper hooks and rollers for the vehicle's front end.

Now I'm planning body panel detailing like door seams, hood seam lines, and mud flaps using thin dark boxes positioned along the body and door bones, then moving into writing the actual geometry code with correct paint logic for painted vs flat door panels.

Writing box geometry helpers...

Now I'm working out the wheel assembly loop, naming each wheel by position and side, then building out the tire core, lug decal, hub, and steering joint geometry with their respective offsets and directions.

Next I'm placing the driver figure inside the cab—working out seat, torso, and head positions relative to the cab floor and window opening so the seated figure sits correctly within the visible interior space.

Then I adjust the greenhouse geometry: resizing the roof height and windshield/side bar dimensions so they clear the interior figure while keeping the overall cab proportions coherent, bringing the total vehicle height to roughly 3.85.

For the driver's head, I'm positioning it slightly offset from center, sizing a helmet box with a red shell, and designing a pixel-art face plane for the visor with a dark band and small eye details facing forward.

I'll skip adding a passenger and place the dashboard box behind the windshield at the right height. For the antenna, I'm deciding to leave it out to avoid pushing the overall height too far up, then finalizing the imports needed for the file—THREE, the builder helpers, pixel art/texture utilities—while being careful to avoid unused variable errors.

Now I'm defining the body paint logic with a gradient of blues shifted by height and normal direction, adding mud spattering near the rocker panels and occasional light fleck highlights, plus a separate mud color ramp for the lower body. I'm also setting up flat black for the chassis and frame, and a textured tile box for the bed floor liner.

I'm sketching a 16x16 ridged bed-liner texture with darker grooves every few pixels and scattered scratch marks, reused for both the bed floor and underbody panels. For the chassis I'm picking yellow accents for cross members and shock bodies with red springs and chrome highlights, then building out the shock absorbers as layered rods (thick yellow body, thin chrome rod) with torus coils stacked along the shock axis, followed by the four-link suspension geometry on both sides.

Now I'm adding drive shafts and a tie rod connecting the front axle, differential housings as flattened spheres mounted under the chassis, and then shifting up to body panels -- rocker boxes, bed side walls, hood seam lines, door skins, the cab lower box, and A-pillar framing pieces.

For the windshield, I'm calculating the slope angle so the A-pillars tilt backward correctly, deriving a rotation around the x-axis from the pillar's vertical offset to match the glass angle, then placing C-pillars at the rear of the greenhouse and working out the door frame geometry to leave an open window gap between them.

Now I'm laying out the door assembly: hinge joint, lower panel, top bar, front and rear frame bars, plus the mirror box with its arm, door handle, and number plate positioning, keeping the door painted to match the body color.

Moving to the tailgate, I'm setting up its hinge joint and defining the gate panel, chrome trim bar, glowing red tail lights, and a rear plate with a pixel-art texture grid.

Finalizing the data export and returning the root object now.
